name: All-Terrain Vehicle
description: A self-propelled vehicle designed to travel over unimproved terrain that the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles has found unsuitable for public highways and that can't be registered for the road; the definition sets no engine, power or speed limit. A two-wheeled one is also a "dirt bike" under §14-390m, and neither can be an electric bicycle. Defined by Connecticut General Statutes §14-379 and regulated by §§14-380 to 14-390.
restrictions: Designed to travel over unimproved terrain, found by the DMV unsuitable for public highways and not eligible for road registration; no limit on motor power or speed
Excluded from the electric bicycle definition, which leaves out dirt bikes and all-terrain vehicles

Registered with the DMV for three years, with a plate on the rear and its number in reflective characters at least 3 inches tall on each side of the front, and the registration carried while riding; not needed only on land the owner owns or leases
Can't be registered to an owner under 16; a 16- or 17-year-old owner needs parental consent and special financial responsibility insurance
Never ridden on a public highway; a licensed driver may cross one, other than a limited-access highway, at about a right angle after a full stop, yielding to traffic
Needs working brakes and adequate front and rear lights and reflectors

Ridden on someone else's land only with the owner's written permission carried by the rider, or the written permission of the state agency or town that controls public land; never on a railroad right-of-way

No state-managed areas are open to dirt bikes or quads, and riding one on state or town land where it isn't specifically allowed can bring criminal trespass charges; the Army Corps of Engineers' Thomaston Dam is open to two-wheeled trail bikes
Towns may regulate them by ordinance, with fines up to $1,000, $1,500 and $2,000 for first, second and later violations, and seize and forfeit the vehicle, which since 2025 they may also destroy
